papers.title: How do standard time series forecasting benchmarks translate to finance? A broad study of risk adjusted performance
papers.abstract: Forecasting financial asset returns is challenging due to low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity and heavy-tailed distributions. We benchmark 16 deep learning architectures for time series forecasting, including Transformers, State Space Models (SSMs), xLSTMs and recurrent hybrids, on a 15-year daily futures dataset using an end-to-end volatility-targeted Sharpe ratio optimisation task. Our results challenge prevailing assumptions in the literature. Several widely used 'state-of-the-art' architectures, including generic Transformers and SSMs, underperformed a simple AR(1) benchmark in a realistic financial forecasting task. The strongest results came from comparatively simple hybrid approaches using recurrent structures: a Variable Selection Network combined with an LSTM achieved the highest Sharpe ratio, while xLSTM showed the greatest robustness to transaction costs. These findings suggest that success on standard time-series benchmarks does not reliably transfer to finance, and that architectures tailored to the unique properties of asset returns may remain more effective than generic attention-based approaches for financial forecasting.

papers.title: Optimal Size in Market Making under State-Dependent Hawkes Process
papers.abstract: We study market making with a parametric model of executed volume that accounts for quote placement and state-dependent order flow. Executed volume is expressed as the product of an average order size, an exponential demand function, and a Prony-series multiplier depending on quote depth, market-order count constructed from a state-dependent Hawkes model. An approximation result for finite Prony sums on a compact state domain provides a mathematical basis for the representation. An empirical study of limit-order-book data examines the calibrated demand and intensity models, sensitivity to inventory restrictions, and the resulting placement policies. In retrospective evaluations conditional on realised order-flow paths, the selected calibration achieves higher terminal utility than a baseline while respecting the prescribed inventory bound. The comparisons also distinguish the contribution of trading revenues from that of inventory control. The resulting closed-form volume specification takes placement levels as inputs and can therefore be used with alternative quoting rules.

papers.title: Visibility-Graph-Based Relative Strength Indicator for Financial Market Decision-Making
papers.abstract: This study introduces the Visibility-Graph-Based Relative Strength Index (VGRSI), a causal indicator that selects and implicitly weights price increments using backward natural visibility. Independent parameters specify the aggregation window and the backward visibility range. Two aggregation variants use the magnitudes and counts of positive and negative contributions to produce values on a 0--100 scale. The VGRSI was tested in an automated walk-forward experiment based on 30-day optimisation windows followed by {7-day walk-forward windows}. This study covered DJI30, EUR/USD, and XAU/USD over 503 trading days in 2024--2025. {The VGRSI strategy produced positive cumulative net profits for all three instruments, whereas the tested classical-RSI strategy and the VGRSI variant without visibility selection produced cumulative losses under the same walk-forward procedure and trading conditions. Because the analysis covered only three instruments and one historical period, the results should be treated as preliminary.
